extracted.intended_audience: mathematics instructors and teacher-educators (K–12 and postsecondary)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and implementing mathematics instruction that improves learning (via active practice, feedback, participation) while attending to equity and classroom hierarchies. Covers proven learning techniques, program-level evidence, and classroom-level status interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice testing involves working on material in a low-stakes way that is not for a grade. It is far more valuable for learning than alternative activities like re-reading a textbook or studying lecture notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-analysis shows a medium to large effect (g = 0.70, pooled from 272 effect sizes). Solutions to practice problems need not be correct—imperfect practice still benefits learning, and incorrect attempts can have learning benefits. Practice testing should be integrated into a larger program of teacher guidance, feedback, and peer support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributed practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributed practice consists of spreading out learning events over time, rather than consolidating them all at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increases retention of skills and knowledge over time and replicates in mathematics studies. Although ideal spacing is not precisely determined, instructors should encourage spacing study/practice rather than cramming (e.g., revisit earlier sections on future homework).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interleaved practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Interleaved practice is when students work on different types of problems at the same time, rather than only focusing on one skill or problem type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improves performance compared to chunked/blocked practice. Instructors can implement by mixing problems from different sections or revisiting earlier topics in later homework; relatively easy to implement and helps students learn more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-explanation / elaborative interrogation
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-explanation prompts students to explain ideas to themselves in their own words; elaborative interrogation focuses on asking why-questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-analysis found a medium effect size for self-explanation (g = 0.55). Students learn more even if explanations are not fully correct; the process helps consolidate and communicate knowledge and resolve contradictions. Use prompts when reading explanatory text or during problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on passive strategies (summarizing, highlighting, mnemonics, imagery, re-reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarizing, highlighting, keyword mnemonics, imagery for text learning, and re-reading had low efficacy in the reviewed literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These aim to improve retention but lack active processing. Given limited student time, prioritize active strategies (practice testing, distributed practice, interleaving, self-explanation) over passive ones like re-reading or highlighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional processes are more impactful than curriculum or CAI
rubrics_metrics.description: Classroom instructional-process interventions (focused on changing instruction) had larger impacts (e.g., d = 0.33 in elementary studies) than mathematics curricula or computer-assisted instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective instructional-process programs use research-based teaching and learning strategies that engage students with peers (e.g., cooperative learning, mastery learning, classroom management, and deliberate direct instruction that includes instructor guidance followed by practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Active learning improves undergraduate STEM outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Active learning describes student-centered teaching techniques where students do activities or discussions rather than listen to pure lecture; meta-analysis (225 studies) found g = 0.47 and much higher failure rates under pure lecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors should incorporate active engagement techniques in postsecondary mathematics; recognize that most K–12 classrooms already include some student practice, whereas pure lecture dominates in higher education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active learning can exacerbate inequities without explicit attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Although active learning increases learning in the aggregate, it can reproduce or exacerbate inequities (by race, gender, prior preparation) if instructors do not intentionally attend to equity with social-marker specificity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume 'for all' approaches will close gaps. Use intentional, targeted practices to disrupt hierarchies and ensure participation opportunities are equitably distributed across social groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice, feedback, and participation as foundational principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Three key reasons why participation is foundational: 1) practice supports learning, 2) feedback supports learning, and 3) participation promotes identity and belonging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design courses to provide ample practice opportunities, timely formative feedback (from instructors and peers), and participation structures that build student belonging and mathematics identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback as a cornerstone of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback helps learners establish where they are relative to their learning goals and figure out how to get there; a large body of evidence documents its importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement formative assessment practices and provide feedback from instructors and peers. Peer feedback is generally positive for learning and is naturally supported in active learning classrooms (pair-share, small groups, whole-class discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation promotes belonging and identity development
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' sense of belonging is crucial to persistence and success; participation in community of peers enhances belonging and helps develop identities as mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create community and meaningful engagement opportunities. Be aware of forces (e.g., racism, anti-Blackness) that shape experiences and work to counteract exclusionary dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-ability treatment (Complex Instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame tasks as requiring diverse skills that all students will have some of, but none will have all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing sets expectation of multiple forms of competence and makes it easier to use status interventions (e.g., assigning competence) to reduce participation gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group-worthy tasks (Complex Instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tasks that engage students in deep learning problems that require multiple minds to meaningfully engage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because these tasks require diverse competences, they make it easier for productive ideas from many students to emerge; they support equitable participation and deeper learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group roles (Complex Instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Support delegation of authority to students by assigning group roles to help equitable engagement within small groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use roles to structure collaboration and ensure that different students have clear responsibilities that distribute participation opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigning competence (Complex Instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly elevate the status of students perceived as low status by highlighting their meaningful contributions in public spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly acknowledge and attribute competence to lower-status students to change perceptions and increase their participation and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement status interventions with attention to social-marker specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex Instruction can reproduce inequities if implemented in a colorblind way; attention to race, gender, disability, and other identities is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine Complex Instruction strategies with data and targeted attention to specific minoritized groups (e.g., disaggregated analyses) to avoid unintentionally reproducing inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use observation tools and disaggregated data (EQUIP) to guide equity interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: An observation tool (EQUIP) and professional development methods grounded in disaggregated student data can reliably produce changes to patterns of inequity in student participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and disaggregate participation and outcome data by social markers (race, gender, disability) and use these data to drive targeted instructional changes and professional development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program evaluation criteria for classroom studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Robust meta-analyses considered studies that had randomized or matched samples, were at least 12 weeks long, and had outcome measures independent of the intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing evidence for instructional programs, prioritize randomized/matched designs, sufficient duration, and independent outcome measures to ensure trustworthy estimates of impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pure lecture as a default
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure lecture produces lower learning outcomes and higher failure rates compared to active learning, yet it remains prevalent for systemic and personal reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors should move away from pure lecture toward active engagement practices, recognizing the additional effort and institutional constraints this change may require.
